reader_summary.headline: As I've written in past memos.
reader_summary.overview: As I've written in past memos, I have an indelible recollection of the first book I read as a Wharton freshman in 1963. The book was Decisions Under Uncertainty, Drilling Decisions by Oil and Gas Operators, by C. Jackson-Grason, Jr., who, in 1971, would take on the role of Price-Zar in the Nixon administration's efforts to get inflation under control.

key_points.text: The best and most lasting thing I took away from Grayson's book, and the first thing I remember learning in college.
key_points.evidence_quote: The best and most lasting thing I took away from Grayson's book, and the first thing I remember learning in college, was the observation that you can't tell the quality of a decision from the outcome.

key_points.text: This revelation had a profound influence on me as a 17-year-old and represented the first critical building block in my understanding of how the world works..
key_points.evidence_quote: This revelation had a profound influence on me as a 17-year-old and represented the first critical building block in my understanding of how the world works.

key_points.text: As Grayson explained, you make the best decision you can, based on what you know.
key_points.evidence_quote: As Grayson explained, you make the best decision you can, based on what you know, but the success of your decision will be heavily influenced by A, relevant information you may lack, and B, luck or randomness.

key_points.text: Because of these two factors, well-thought-out decisions may fail, and poor decisions may succeed.
key_points.evidence_quote: Because of these two factors, well-thought-out decisions may fail, and poor decisions may succeed.

thesis: Howard Marks argues that the quality of a decision cannot be judged by its outcome because success is heavily influenced by luck and missing information. He illustrates this principle by drawing parallels between investing and games of chance like blackjack and backgammon, where skill involves understanding probabilities and processes rather than relying on luck or guaranteed strategies.
